summary:
This run covered 12 evals (22 iterations). Two evals (neg-live-outage-503, neg-kb-embedding-dimension) were should_trigger:false negative tests and were skipped from scoring — both variants correctly did not fire on them (trigger_fired 100%), but no other dimensions apply there.

Of the 10 scored evals, the trigger fired 100% of the time in all cases for both variants — the behavior under test reliably activated.

**Expected output match:** with_skill met the expected output in 10/10 scored evals (all high or medium confidence). without_skill met it in only 3/10 (quota-headroom, per-model-cost-breakdown, cost-global-vs-geographic-profile, delete-pt-stays-read-only — actually 4/10), failing expected output in the remaining 6 evals (cost-throttle-default-quota, quota-lookup-by-code, tokens-per-day-quota, billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained, mantle-usage-type-is-not-mantle-endpoint, invocation-log-retention), all at high confidence except one medium. This is a consistent and fairly high-confidence pattern across many independent evals, not a single outlier.

**Per-assertion detail:** with_skill's assertion pass rate was at or near 100% in 8 of 10 evals, dropping only on per-model-cost-breakdown (60%) and cost-global-vs-geographic-profile (67%). without_skill's assertion pass rates were lower across the board, ranging from 20% (mantle-usage-type) to 100% (none reached 100%; quota-headroom was its high point at 83%). Several assertions passed for both variants (e.g., "quotes the applicable quota value," "chooses cross-Region quota form," "distinguishes billed token mismatch") — these are not discriminating. A recurring assertion that failed for both variants across several evals is the one requiring findings to carry an LLM-COST/PT/INV check-ids with severity — this suggests that specific check/finding-labeling behavior needs work independent of which variant is used. One assertion ("does not fabricate forward pricing," on per-model-cost-breakdown) and one ("gives concrete way to confirm global profile," on cost-global-vs-geographic-profile) passed for without_skill but failed for with_skill, showing the pattern isn't fully one-sided. A recurring, fairly consistent finding is that without_skill exposed a raw 12-digit account ID in several evals where with_skill did not (6 of 10 scored evals), a specific and repeatable difference.

**Quality comparisons:** Of the 10 scored evals, only 5 had quality pairs evaluated (others were skipped as non-comparable). Among those 5, with_skill was favored in the majority of criteria (accuracy, completeness, actionability) in 4 of 5 (per-model-cost-breakdown, cost-global-vs-geographic-profile, delete-pt-stays-read-only, and a 2-1 split on quota-headroom where without_skill was favored only on actionability). These quality judgments carry medium-to-high confidence.

**Runtime and cost:** Results are mixed and large in magnitude. In several evals, without_skill was much faster/cheaper (e.g., cost-throttle-default-quota: with_skill 1m51s/$0.93 vs without_skill 24s/$0.21; per-model-cost-breakdown: with_skill 1m40s/$0.84 vs without_skill 13s/$0.11). In other evals, without_skill was dramatically slower and more expensive (tokens-per-day-quota: with_skill 15s/$0.13 vs without_skill 11m6s/$5.53; quota-headroom: with_skill 57s/$0.48 vs without_skill 10m53s/$5.42). There is no consistent direction — without_skill is sometimes much cheaper/faster and sometimes much slower/costlier than with_skill, so runtime/cost cannot be summarized as a stable advantage for either side. Context window utilization was consistently somewhat higher for with_skill (6-12%) than without_skill (4-7%), though both are low overall with no compactions.

**Output consistency:** This dimension was not populated (null) for both variants across all evals, so no run-to-run variability data is available.

**Overall pattern:** Across the scored evals, with_skill met the expected output and passed more individual assertions more consistently than without_skill, and quality judgments (where available, on only half the evals) also favored with_skill on accuracy/completeness/actionability in most cases. without_skill occasionally matched or beat with_skill on specific assertions, cost, or speed, and the cost/runtime relationship between the two varies unpredictably eval-to-eval rather than favoring one side systematically. A few assertions (notably the finding/check-id labeling requirement) failed for both variants everywhere they appeared, indicating a shared gap rather than a between-variant difference. The account-ID exposure difference and the expected-output gap for without_skill recur across many independent evals, which raises confidence that these are real patterns rather than noise, but the lack of output-consistency data and partial quality-pair coverage (only 5 of 10) means the overall picture is incomplete.

- Two assertions favored with_skill and failed for without_skill: comparing observed usage against quota (rather than assuming quota is the problem), and distinguishing sustained under-provisioning from burstiness that retries would absorb. Both failures for without_skill were rated high confidence.
- One assertion favored without_skill and failed for with_skill: that any findings raised carry a proper check-id and severity and rest only on cited evidence (also high confidence in both directions).
- One regex-based assertion (no raw 12-digit account ID exposed) passed for with_skill and failed for without_skill.
Overall assertion pass rates were 4/5 (80%) for with_skill vs 2/5 (40%) for without_skill, but this aggregate masks a mixed picture: one assertion where neither variant's result differs, one where without_skill actually outperformed with_skill (evidence-citation/finding-quality), and one where with_skill exposed a raw account ID — a specific, concrete regression on a security-relevant check.

Runtime and cost: with_skill took much longer (avg ~1m51s) and cost more (~$0.93) than without_skill (~24s, ~$0.21) — roughly a 4-5x difference in both time and cost. Context window utilization was also higher for with_skill (11.8%) vs without_skill (4.3%), with no compaction for either.

Quality comparison: no comparable pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so no direct quality-preference signal is available beyond the assertions above.

Output consistency: not available for either variant (null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, this is a single-task, single-run comparison, so findings should be treated as indicative rather than conclusive. Variant_a met more assertions and the expected output on this run, including a concrete account-ID-exposure difference in its favor, but it took substantially longer and cost more, and it failed the assertion about citing evidence properly for findings, which without_skill passed. This represents a tradeoff between speed/cost and certain correctness/safety checks rather than a clean win for either variant.

The one differentiating assertion — showing the quota in a table with name, code, applied value, and adjustability — passed for with_skill and failed for without_skill, and this was judged with high confidence, so it's a reasonably solid distinction in formatting/completeness of output.

Quality comparison: Across the single pair evaluated, with_skill was favored on 2 of 3 criteria (accuracy, completeness) and without_skill was favored on 1 (actionability), with no criteria rated comparable. Confidence in this comparison is medium, and it's based on only one pair, so it should be treated as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Runtime and cost: with_skill completed in about 57 seconds at an average cost of $0.48, while without_skill took about 10 minutes 53 seconds at an average cost of $5.42 — a substantial difference in both speed and cost for this task. Neither run exceeded the defined runtime threshold in the runtime comparison metric. Context window utilization was low for both (8.8% for with_skill, 5.7% for without_skill) with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: No consistency data was available for either variant (marked null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, this is a single-task comparison where with_skill matched or exceeded without_skill on the assertion pass rate and on two of three quality criteria, and did so with notably lower runtime and cost, while without_skill scored better on one quality criterion (actionability). Given the very small sample size (one pair), low confidence on one assertion, and missing consistency data, these results should be treated as a limited, single-instance signal rather than a definitive comparison.

cost-global-vs-geographic-profile.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about Bedrock cross-Region inference pricing/profiles. The trigger behavior fired in the one run tested.

Both variants met the overall "expected output" criterion (1/1), though the confidence behind that judgment is only "medium" for both, so this agreement should be read as a fairly weak signal rather than a strong one.

On the detailed assertions (6 checks, single run each), with_skill passed 4/6 and without_skill passed 3/6. Looking at individual assertions rather than the aggregate:
- Two assertions passed for both variants (explaining the ~10% global cross-Region pricing discount, and sourcing actual rates from the Price List API/pricing page/Cost Explorer rather than memory) — these don't differentiate the variants.
- One assertion (requiring findings to carry proper LLM-COST/LLM-PT/LLM-INV check-IDs with severities) failed for both variants, suggesting this is a weak spot in the underlying behavior/assertion rather than a difference between the two.
- One assertion split in with_skill's favor: explaining that a global profile can route to any supported commercial Region and naming the SCP/residency implication — with_skill passed, without_skill failed.
- One assertion split in without_skill's favor: giving a concrete way to confirm a global profile exists (ListInferenceProfiles/GetInferenceProfile) — without_skill passed, with_skill failed.
- One assertion (no raw 12-digit account ID exposed) passed for with_skill and failed for without_skill — a potential sensitive-data exposure difference, though based on only one run.

On quality, with_skill was favored over without_skill on all three judged criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness) for the single pair evaluated, with high average confidence in that judgment — though this rests on just one paired comparison, so it's a single data point rather than a broad trend.

On efficiency, without_skill was notably faster (48s vs 1m34s) and cheaper ($0.40 vs $0.78), with lower context-window utilization (7.3% vs 11.1%); neither used any context compaction. One run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the runtime comparison (medium confidence), but with only one pair evaluated this is a limited sample.

Output consistency across repeated runs was not available (null) for either variant, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, the picture is a tradeoff rather than a clear-cut outcome: with_skill showed higher per-assertion pass rate and was favored on all quality criteria in the single compared pair, including passing an account-ID exposure check that without_skill failed, while without_skill ran substantially faster and cheaper and uniquely satisfied the concrete profile-verification assertion. All findings here are based on a single run/pair, several with only medium confidence, so the sample size is small and these results should be treated as preliminary rather than definitive.

delete-pt-stays-read-only.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task, so all findings rest on just one trial per variant (and one quality-comparison pair) — confidence in any difference is therefore limited.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected (1/1), and both with_skill and without_skill met the expected output on their one trial (1/1, 100%). with_skill's expected-output judgment was made with high confidence, while without_skill's was medium confidence, meaning the measurement behind without_skill's result is somewhat weaker even though the pass rate is the same.

Assertions (6 checks, 1 trial each): Four of six assertions behaved identically for both variants — three always passed (not deleting throughput itself and leaving the action to the user; checking/reporting whether the throughput exists; mentioning moving traffic first or that a commitment bills until term end) and one always failed (raising findings with proper LLM-COST/LLM-PT/LLM-INV check-IDs and severities, supported by evidence). Since these four are identical across variants, they don't differentiate the two systems — though the always-failing one flags a shared weakness (or an assertion/behavior that may need rework) worth attention regardless of variant. The "Gives the delete command for the user" check passed for both as well. The one differentiating assertion — "No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed" — passed for with_skill and failed for without_skill, the only case where the two variants diverged. Overall assertion pass rate was 5/6 (83%) for with_skill versus 4/6 (67%) for without_skill, driven entirely by this single assertion.

Quality comparison: Across the one evaluated pair, with_skill was favored on all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with without_skill favored on none, at medium average confidence. With only one pair evaluated, this is a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was faster (~8s vs ~11s) and cheaper (~$0.07 vs ~$0.09), with lower context-window utilization (4.5% vs 6.8%); neither had any compaction events, and neither run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold. This is a modest efficiency advantage for without_skill.

Output consistency: Not measured (null) for both variants, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, the two variants performed identically on most assertions and on the expected-output check, with with_skill showing an edge on the account-ID-exposure assertion and on the single quality comparison, while without_skill ran somewhat faster and cheaper. Given the single-trial, single-pair nature of this evaluation, these differences should be viewed as early signals rather than conclusive results.
